t: ₹50,000 is deposited at 8% per annum compound interest. The amount after 3 years is (1.08³ = 1.259712)
e: Amount = 50,000 × 1.259712 = ₹62,986. Simple interest would give only ₹62,000, the difference being interest on interest.

t: If the effective rate of interest is 5% per annum, the corresponding rate of discount d is
e: d = i/(1 + i) = 0.05/1.05 = 0.047619, i.e. 4.76%. The discount rate is interest paid in advance, so it is always slightly below i.

t: At 10% per annum, find the present value of two payments of ₹1,00,000 each, due at the end of years 3 and 4. (v³ = 0.75131, v⁴ = 0.68301)
e: PV = 1,00,000 × (0.75131 + 0.68301) = ₹1,43,432. This is a deferred annuity-certain of two payments.

t: What lump sum invested at 6% per annum will provide a perpetuity of ₹6,000 payable at the end of each year?
e: PV of a perpetuity in arrears = payment / i = 6,000 / 0.06 = ₹1,00,000; the interest alone meets each payment without touching capital.

t: Given l₂₅ = 98,000, l₂₆ = 97,900 and l₂₇ = 97,790, the probability that a life aged 25 dies in the second year (between ages 26 and 27) is
e: ₁|q₂₅ = (l₂₆ − l₂₇)/l₂₅ = 110/98,000 = 0.00112. Dividing by l₂₆ instead would give q₂₆, the rate for a life who has already reached 26.

t: If q₅₀ = 0.006 and q₅₁ = 0.007, the probability that a life aged 50 survives two years is
e: ₂p₅₀ = p₅₀ × p₅₁ = 0.994 × 0.993 = 0.987042. Simply subtracting the two q's (0.987) ignores the compounding of survival.

t: Under the uniform distribution of deaths assumption, with l_x = 10,000 and l_{x+1} = 9,900, the central rate of mortality m_x is approximately
e: m_x = d_x / L_x where L_x ≈ (l_x + l_{x+1})/2 = 9,950; m_x = 100/9,950 = 0.01005, slightly above q_x = 0.0100 because the exposed-to-risk is the mid-year population.

t: With N₄₀ = 40,000 and D₄₀ = 2,000, the value of a whole life immediate annuity of ₹1 per annum (first payment at age 41) on a life aged 40 is
e: a₄₀ = N₄₁ / D₄₀ = (N₄₀ − D₄₀)/D₄₀ = 38,000/2,000 = 19. The annuity-due ä₄₀ = N₄₀/D₄₀ = 20 is one more, representing the immediate payment.

t: ₹10,000 is invested at 6% per annum compound interest. What is the accumulated amount at the end of 2 years?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Accumulated value = 10,000 × (1.06)² = 10,000 × 1.1236 = ₹11,236. ₹11,200 is the simple-interest figure, which ignores interest on interest.

t: For a life aged 30, M₃₀ = 900, M₅₀ = 600 and D₃₀ = 4,500. The net single premium for a 20-year term assurance of ₹15,00,000 is
An immediate annuity of ₹10,000 per annum payable yearly in arrears for life is purchased by a person aged 60. If a₆₀ = 11.5, the net purchase price is
e: Purchase price = annual amount × a₆₀ = 10,000 × 11.5 = ₹1,15,000. Expense loading would be added for the office price.

t: A net annual premium is ₹5,000. Initial expenses of ₹3,000 are to be spread over the premium-paying term (ä = 12) and renewal expenses are 4% of the office premium. The office premium is approximately
e: P' = (5,000 + 3,000/12)/(1 − 0.04) = 5,250/0.96 = ₹5,469. The initial expense is converted to a level annual amount by dividing by ä and the percentage loading by dividing by (1 − k).

t: An office annual premium of ₹12,000 contains a loading of 25% of the net premium. The net premium is
e: Office premium = net × 1.25, so net = 12,000/1.25 = ₹9,600. Dividing by 0.75 (₹16,000) would wrongly treat the loading as 25% of the office premium.

t: Half-yearly premiums are more than one-half of the annual premium for the same policy chiefly because of
o: loss of interest and additional collection expenses
e: Collecting in instalments defers part of the premium (loss of interest) and multiplies collection and accounting costs, so a frequency loading is applied to instalment premiums.

t: If A₄₀ = 0.25 and ä₄₀ = 15, the net annual premium for a whole life assurance of ₹3,00,000 on (40) payable throughout life is
On a retrospective basis, the accumulated value of net premiums paid per surviving policy is ₹30,000 and the accumulated cost of assurance per surviving policy is ₹6,000. The policy value is
e: Retrospective reserve = accumulated premiums − accumulated cost of claims (both per survivor) = 30,000 − 6,000 = ₹24,000.

t: If p₄₀ = 0.998 and p₃₅ = 0.999 for two independent lives, the probability that the joint life status (35, 40) survives one year is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). p_xy = p_x × p_y = 0.999 × 0.998 = 0.997002. The joint status fails on the first death, so both must survive.

t: A 15-year endowment of ₹5,00,000 on (45) has net premium 0.055 per ₹1. After 5 years, A₅₀:₁₀ = 0.62 and ä₅₀:₁₀ = 8.0. The prospective net premium reserve is
For an endowment assurance the net premium reserve can be written as ₜV = 1 − ä_{x+t:n−t}/ä_{x:n}. If ä₄₀:₂₀ = 13 and ä₅₀:₁₀ = 8, the reserve per ₹1 after 10 years is
e: ₁₀V = 1 − 8/13 = 1 − 0.6154 = 0.3846. This annuity-ratio formula follows from A = 1 − dä applied at entry and at duration t.

t: A policy has a sum assured of ₹10,00,000 and a reserve of ₹2,40,000. The death strain at risk (sum at risk) is
e: Sum at risk = sum assured − reserve = 10,00,000 − 2,40,000 = ₹7,60,000; on death the insurer must find this amount over and above the reserve already held.

t: The net premium reserve of a level-premium temporary (term) assurance over its term
o: rises steadily to the sum assured
rises and then falls back to zero at expiry
e: Level premiums exceed the rising cost of cover early (building a small reserve) and fall short later (reserve runs down), so the reserve rises then falls to zero at expiry when no benefit remains.

t: Immediately after issue, the net premium reserve of a single-premium whole life assurance equals
e: No future premiums are receivable, so the prospective reserve is simply the PV of the benefit, which at issue is the net single premium just received.

t: For lives (x) and (y), a_x = 14, a_y = 16 and the joint-life annuity a_xy = 10. The last-survivor annuity a_{x̄y} is
e: a_{x̄y} = a_x + a_y − a_xy = 14 + 16 − 10 = 20. The last-survivor annuity must exceed each single-life annuity.

t: Using the same values (a_y = 16, a_xy = 10), the reversionary annuity payable to (y) after the death of (x) has value
e: a_{x|y} = a_y − a_xy = 16 − 10 = 6: payments to y while alive, less payments during the period both are alive.

t: If q_x = 0.01 and q_y = 0.02 for independent lives, the probability that both die within one year is
e: P(both die) = q_x × q_y = 0.01 × 0.02 = 0.0002, which is also the probability that the last-survivor status fails within the year.

t: The primary purpose of a life insurer fixing a retention limit is to
o: reduce fluctuations in claims experience from large individual risks
e: By ceding amounts above its retention the insurer limits the effect of any one large death claim, stabilising its mortality experience relative to its free assets.

t: An insurer retains ₹30 lakh per life and has a surplus treaty of 5 lines. A policy for ₹80 lakh is written. The amount ceded to the treaty is
e: Treaty capacity is 5 × 30 = ₹150 lakh, which comfortably covers the surplus; ceded = 80 − 30 = ₹50 lakh with ₹30 lakh retained.

t: Under a compound reversionary bonus of 4% per annum, a sum assured of ₹1,00,000 grows after 2 years to
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Compound bonus is declared on sum assured plus previously attached bonuses: 1,00,000 × 1.04² = ₹1,08,160. ₹1,08,000 is the simple-bonus figure.

t: Which item is NOT normally required in the policy record used for valuation?
e: Valuation needs plan, term, sum assured, bonuses, premium, dates of birth and commencement and status; the agent's name is irrelevant to the liability.

t: In a gross premium valuation of a policy, PV of future benefits is ₹8,00,000, PV of future expenses ₹1,00,000 and PV of future office premiums ₹6,00,000. The reserve is
e: Gross premium reserve = PV benefits + PV expenses − PV office premiums = 8,00,000 + 1,00,000 − 6,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

t: A net premium valuation using a lower rate of interest than the premium basis is described as
o: identical to a gross premium valuation
stronger, deferring the emergence of surplus
e: A lower valuation interest rate produces larger reserves, which is a stronger (more conservative) basis; the surplus held back emerges later as the policies run off.

t: For a group of policies the reserve just after the premium at the start of the year is ₹10,000 and at the end of the year ₹12,000. The mean reserve used in a mid-year grouped valuation is
e: Mean reserve = (initial reserve + terminal reserve)/2 = (10,000 + 12,000)/2 = ₹11,000, appropriate when policy anniversaries are spread evenly over the year.

t: A one-year group term policy with annual premium ₹12,00,000 commenced on 1 April. At a valuation on 31 December of the same year, the unexpired risk reserve (ignoring expenses) is
e: Three months of cover remain of the twelve purchased, so the unexpired premium reserve = 12,00,000 × 3/12 = ₹3,00,000.

t: A life fund of ₹50 crore is valued at 6% interest but actually earns 8% during the year. The interest surplus for the year is approximately
e: Interest surplus ≈ (actual − valuation rate) × fund = (0.08 − 0.06) × 50 crore = ₹1 crore.

t: A participating policy of ₹2,00,000 receives a compound reversionary bonus of 3% per annum for 3 years. The sum assured with bonuses becomes
Deduction for health insurance premium under Section 80D for an individual below 60 years (self and family) is up to:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹25,000; ₹50,000 where the insured is a senior citizen; an additional ₹25,000/₹50,000 for parents.

t: Under a 90:10 distribution, a participating fund declares a distributable surplus of ₹45 crore. The shareholders' maximum share is
e: Shareholders may take not more than 10% of the surplus distributed to policyholders' bonuses in the participating fund: 10% × 45 crore = ₹4.5 crore.

t: At the surrender date a policy's asset share is ₹60,000, its reserve is ₹55,000 and the surrender value paid is ₹50,000. The surrender profit to the fund is
e: Surrender profit = asset share − surrender value = 60,000 − 50,000 = ₹10,000, the amount the departing policyholder leaves behind for the fund.

t: Asset shares are used by a life office mainly to
o: set surrender values and check the fairness of bonus rates
e: Asset shares show what each policy has actually contributed, so they guide equitable surrender values and bonus (payout) levels; statutory reserves and premiums are set by other methods.

t: A policy made paid-up for ₹80,000 is surrendered immediately after. If the surrender value is paid as the present value of the paid-up benefit with A₅₀:₁₀ = 0.65, the surrender value is
e: Surrender value = paid-up sum assured × A factor = 80,000 × 0.65 = ₹52,000.

t: A policyholder asks to extend the term of a 15-year endowment to 20 years, keeping the sum assured unchanged. Other things equal, the revised annual premium will
o: be payable as a single premium
e: A longer term spreads the saving element over more premiums and defers the maturity benefit, so the premium per annum falls; the reserve at the date of alteration is carried into the new contract.

t: Which of the following is the main expense risk for a life insurer with a large block of small, long-term policies?
o: Expense inflation exceeding the inflation assumed in the loading
e: Fixed per-policy expenses on small long-term policies are vulnerable to inflation; if expenses rise faster than the loadings assumed, expense losses emerge.

t: The symbol ä (a-double-dot) in actuarial notation denotes an annuity in which payments are made
o: at the beginning of each period
at the end of each period
e: ä_n denotes an annuity-due, payable in advance at the start of each period; a_n denotes an immediate annuity payable in arrears. The relation ä_n = (1 + i) a_n holds.

t: The curtate expectation of life e_x is defined as
o: the number of complete years expected to be lived after age x
the exact number of years expected to be lived after age x, including fractions
the age at which l_x falls to half
the sum of q_x over all future ages
e: e_x = Σ l_{x+t}/l_x (t = 1, 2, …) gives the expected number of complete future years; the complete expectation e°x ≈ e_x + ½ includes the fraction of the year of death.

t: Why are office premiums for a participating (with-profits) policy higher than for an otherwise identical non-participating policy?
o: They include a loading to fund future bonuses
Mortality is heavier for with-profits lives
e: With-profits office premiums contain a bonus loading so that the expected surplus can support the bonuses to be declared; mortality and expense assumptions are otherwise similar.

t: For a term assurance, the premium rate per ₹1,000 sum assured is reduced for large sum assured bands mainly because
o: fixed per-policy expenses form a smaller proportion of the premium
e: Per-policy fixed expenses (issue, administration) do not grow with sum assured, so the expense loading per ₹1,000 falls as the sum assured rises; insurers reflect this through sum-assured rebates.

t: Third-party insurance is compulsory for a motor vehicle used in a public place under which section of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 146 makes TP cover compulsory; Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt).

t: The reserve for a regular-premium endowment assurance approaches which value at maturity?
e: As the maturity date approaches the probability of payment tends to 1 and the discount period to zero, so the reserve rises to the sum assured (plus attached bonuses) at maturity.

t: In a select mortality table the symbol q_[x]+1 denotes the rate of mortality of a life
o: now aged x+1 who was selected one year ago
now aged x who was selected one year ago
now aged x+1 selected at age x+1
e: Square brackets show the age at selection; q_[x]+1 is for a life selected at x, now aged x+1, one year after selection. After the select period it merges into the ultimate rate q_{x+1}.

t: Under the net premium method of valuation, the premium valued is
o: the office premium less actual expenses
the net premium on the valuation basis
e: The net premium method values a net premium computed on the valuation mortality and interest basis, independent of the office premium; the margin between office and net premiums emerges as future surplus.
